paragraphs.title: Who Is Worthy to Be in God's Presence

easy.explanation: The verse begins, “LORD, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?”
easy.q: To whom is the question addressed at the beginning of the psalm?

answers: Who shall abide in God's tabernacle
easy.explanation: The question asks who shall abide in the LORD's tabernacle.
easy.q: What does David ask about the worthy person?

easy.explanation: The verse asks, “who shall dwell in thy holy hill?”
easy.q: Where else does the verse ask who shall dwell?

answers: Both describe being in God's presence
One concerns war and the other commerce
One describes a person and the other an animal
medium.explanation: Both expressions describe dwelling near or in the presence of God.
medium.q: What do abiding in God's tabernacle and dwelling in His holy hill have in common?

medium.explanation: The verse mentions the LORD's tabernacle and His holy hill.
medium.q: How many places of dwelling are mentioned in the verse?

answers: To introduce the subject of the psalm
medium.explanation: The questions introduce the subject: who is worthy to be in God's presence.
medium.q: What is the purpose of the two questions in the verse?

challenge.explanation: Both questions begin with the word “who.”
challenge.q: Which word is repeated at the beginning of both questions and emphasizes the search for the worthy person?

answers: The qualities will be explained afterward
The verse has already answered everything
challenge.explanation: The first verse raises the question, and the following verses describe the worthy person's qualities.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the verse asks a question before describing the person's qualities?

answers: Who is worthy to be near God
Who is worthy to become wealthy
Who is worthy to lead an army
challenge.explanation: The verse concerns the person who may abide in God's tabernacle and dwell in His holy hill.
challenge.q: Which statement best summarizes the idea of the verse?

paragraphs.title: Integrity, Truth, and Responsibility Toward Others

easy.explanation: The verse says, “He that walketh uprightly.”
easy.q: How does the worthy person walk?

easy.explanation: The verse says that he “worketh righteousness.”
easy.q: What does the worthy person work?

easy.explanation: The verse says that he “doeth” no evil “to his neighbour.”
easy.q: What does the worthy person not do to his neighbour?

answers: He does not gossip or speak maliciously
medium.explanation: The expression describes avoiding harmful or malicious speech about another person.
medium.q: What does “backbiteth not with his tongue” mean in context?

medium.explanation: The verses describe truthful speech together with avoiding speech that harms others.
medium.q: How are speaking truth and avoiding backbiting connected?

answers: Both describe protecting and respecting others
medium.explanation: Both expressions emphasize avoiding harm and disgrace toward one's neighbour.
medium.q: What do “doeth evil to his neighbour” and “taketh up a reproach against his neighbour” have in common?

answers: Integrity is required in both actions and speech
challenge.explanation: The verse presents upright conduct, righteous deeds, and truthful speech as parts of the same character.
challenge.q: What conclusion follows from combining walking uprightly, working righteousness, and speaking truth?

answers: Moral responsibility includes how one treats other people
challenge.explanation: The verses show that righteousness includes avoiding evil and reproach against one's neighbour.
challenge.q: What can be learned from the repeated reference to a neighbour?

answers: An upright way, righteous action and truth, then responsibility toward others
challenge.explanation: The verses move from the person's character and actions to his speech and treatment of others.
challenge.q: Which order best describes the ideas in these verses?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “he honoureth them that fear the LORD.”
easy.q: Whom does the worthy person honor?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “nor taketh reward against the innocent.”
easy.q: What does the person not take against the innocent?

easy.explanation: The psalm concludes, “He that doeth these things shall never be moved.”
easy.q: What is said about the person who does these things?

medium.explanation: In this context, usury refers to charging interest on money lent.
medium.q: What does “usury” mean in the phrase “putteth not out his money to usury”?

answers: He keeps his oath even when it costs him
medium.explanation: The person keeps his sworn commitment even when doing so causes him personal loss or pain.
medium.q: What does the phrase “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” mean?

answers: He does not use money to exploit others or corrupt justice
He avoids all contact with people
He seeks profit in every situation
medium.explanation: The verse presents refusing unjust financial gain and bribery as evidence of moral conduct.
medium.q: How do avoiding usury and refusing a reward against the innocent show the person's moral way?

answers: He rejects what is morally vile and honors what is worthy
challenge.explanation: The verse describes moral discernment: the vile person is rejected, while those who fear the LORD are honored.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between a vile person being contemned and those who fear the LORD being honored?

answers: Doing these things results in never being moved
Standing firmly is unrelated to conduct
These actions cause the person to leave his way
challenge.explanation: The final sentence says that the person who does these things “shall never be moved.”
challenge.q: What connection does the ending make between these actions and standing firmly?

challenge.explanation: All three actions show loyalty to moral principles even when another choice might bring personal benefit.
challenge.q: What quality is shared by keeping an oath, avoiding usury, and refusing a reward against the innocent?
